title: 12th Grade Language Arts — English IV
subtitle: Advanced Universal 36-Week Senior College, Career, Civic & Capstone Literacy Course

units.title: Senior Scholar Foundations & Independent Literacy
units.essential: What habits distinguish an independent reader, writer, researcher, and ethical communicator?
units.summary: Establish a senior-year baseline through high-complexity reading, evidence-based interpretation, academic vocabulary, revision, source ethics, responsible technology use, and a documented growth plan.
units.assessment: Senior diagnostic portfolio with literary and informational analysis, convention editing, source-use audit, and individualized mastery plan.

units.title: Epic, Tragedy & World Literary Foundations
units.essential: How do foundational stories and dramatic forms continue to shape modern ideas, conflicts, and identities?
units.summary: Study epic, myth, tragedy, archetype, allusion, character choice, dramatic structure, and adaptation across cultures and periods.
units.assessment: Comparative literary analysis tracing a foundational pattern, theme, or form into a later world text or adaptation.

units.title: Poetry, Voice, Form & Advanced Interpretation
units.essential: How do poets transform language, form, sound, ambiguity, and historical pressure into meaning?
units.summary: Evaluate major poets and global poetic traditions through speaker, form, syntax, image, sound, figurative language, context, translation, and competing interpretations.
units.assessment: Unseen-poem analysis, comparative poetry essay, recitation or performance, and contextual commentary.

units.title: Rhetoric, Public Discourse & Ethical Persuasion
units.essential: How do language, structure, credibility, emotion, timing, and evidence shape public judgment?
units.summary: Evaluate rhetorical situations, classical and global rhetorical traditions, speeches, essays, public documents, civic discourse, oral delivery, and the ethics of persuasion.
units.assessment: Rhetorical analysis, public-address performance, and annotated evaluation of rhetorical choices across texts.

units.title: Argument, Logic, Media & Information Literacy
units.essential: How can citizens distinguish sound reasoning from manipulation in a complex information environment?
units.summary: Compare competing arguments, test evidence, detect fallacies, interpret quantitative information, evaluate news and digital media, and construct fair, evidence-based positions.
units.assessment: Multi-source issue dossier, argument comparison, media-verification lab, deliberative seminar, and formal civic argument.

units.title: Synthesis, Research Design & Midyear Mastery
units.essential: How do researchers transform a difficult question and conflicting evidence into a defensible synthesis?
units.summary: Develop inquiry questions, evaluate source authority and limitations, synthesize literary, informational, visual, and quantitative evidence, and demonstrate cumulative first-semester mastery.
units.assessment: Source-based synthesis essay, research prospectus, cumulative midterm, corrections analysis, and midyear conference.

units.title: Modern & Contemporary World Literature
units.essential: How do modern and contemporary writers represent identity, memory, displacement, power, and social change?
units.summary: Analyze globally diverse short fiction, memoir, essays, translated literature, and postcolonial or diasporic voices with attention to perspective, structure, historical context, and translation.
units.assessment: Comparative global-literature essay and seminar connecting form, context, perspective, and universal themes.

units.title: Language, Power, Culture & Global Issues
units.essential: How do language choices and media forms construct identity, authority, belonging, and public understanding?
units.summary: Study dialect, code-switching, discourse communities, representation, visual rhetoric, documentary and film, adaptation, accessibility, and a globally significant issue.
units.assessment: Comparative oral or multimedia commentary on a global issue, supported by literary and nonliterary evidence.

units.title: Advanced Research & Academic Writing
units.essential: What makes a senior research claim original, responsible, credible, and useful?
units.summary: Conduct sustained research, use databases and advanced search, evaluate scholarship, synthesize disagreements, document sources, analyze data, and draft an academic paper or literary inquiry.
units.assessment: Research question, proposal, annotated bibliography, synthesis matrix, literature review, conference, and documented draft.

units.title: College, Career, Civic & Digital Communication
units.essential: How should a graduate adapt voice, evidence, structure, and medium for consequential real-world audiences?
units.summary: Produce college or scholarship writing, professional correspondence, proposals, résumés, civic communication, explanatory writing, and accessible digital publication while reflecting on ethical technology use.
units.assessment: Postsecondary communication portfolio with personal statement, résumé, professional correspondence, proposal, and accessible multimedia publication.

units.title: Long-Form Literature, Theory & Independent Seminar
units.essential: How can sustained reading and critical lenses deepen or challenge an interpretation of a complete work?
units.summary: Complete a demanding novel or drama, trace motifs and structural development, compare interpretations, apply critical lenses responsibly, and lead an evidence-based seminar.
units.assessment: Long-form reading dossier, independent literary argument, seminar leadership, and oral defense.

units.title: Capstone Inquiry, Graduation Portfolio & Final
units.essential: What body of evidence demonstrates independent readiness for college, career, civic life, and lifelong literacy?
units.summary: Complete a senior capstone, curate and defend a standards-based portfolio, revise representative work, complete a cumulative final, document corrections, and prepare a postsecondary literacy plan.
units.assessment: Senior capstone, graduation portfolio, oral defense, cumulative final examination, corrections, and postsecondary literacy plan.

quiz.question: Which practice best supports independent close reading of a difficult passage?
choices: Use multiple passes to examine comprehension, structure, evidence, context, and uncertainty
Replace the passage with a summary
Ignore unfamiliar words
Read once and accept the first impression
quiz.explanation: Independent advanced reading is deliberate and evidence-based, not dependent on a single first impression.

quiz.question: Which revision record best demonstrates authentic authorship?
choices: A list of page numbers only
A final draft with no process evidence
A log showing drafts, feedback, source use, changes, and reasons for revision
A copied model response
quiz.explanation: Documented decisions and revisions provide credible evidence of authorship and growth.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 01: Senior Diagnostic & Independent Scholar Habits?
choices: read independently, document uncertainty, reason from evidence, revise transparently, and preserve authorship evidence
Choose a conclusion before examining the text or sources
Focus on appearance while ignoring reasoning and accuracy
Rely on a summary without testing evidence
quiz.explanation: This week requires students to read independently, document uncertainty, reason from evidence, revise transparently, and preserve authorship evidence.

quiz.question: English IV · Week 01 (Senior Diagnostic & Independent Scholar Habits): An official archive record confirms who signed an agreement but excludes the experience of affected residents. Which senior-level claim is defensible?
choices: The archive cannot establish any information at all.
The record establishes official terms while leaving broader consent and consequences unsettled.
The absence of residents proves universal opposition.
An official document supplies every perspective automatically.
quiz.explanation: Official provenance does not equal comprehensive representation.

quiz.question: English IV · Week 01 (Senior Diagnostic & Independent Scholar Habits): Which sentence separates institutional record from public reception?
choices: 'The memorandum proves the community accepted the outcome.'
'Institutional records, community acceptance obviously complete.'
'The agreement records; and everyone agreed.'
'The memorandum records the agreement; community acceptance requires additional evidence.'
quiz.explanation: A semicolon joins independently defensible claims while preserving evidentiary limits.

A list of sources

The speaker’s biography only

Shared reform goals prove identical rhetorical strategies.
Different appeals may arise from distinct audience concerns, even when the policy goal is shared.

Adjusting organization, language, evidence, detail, and medium while preserving accuracy
Using the same format in every situation
Avoiding a clear purpose

Removing all source citations
Pretending they do not exist
Representing them accurately and explaining the evidence and reasoning for the speaker’s position

'Anyone worried about the budget must oppose public services.'

A source citation only
An unrelated example
The reasoning that connects evidence to a claim
quiz.explanation: The warrant explains why the evidence supports the claim.

Distort the opposing position
Represent the strongest relevant opposing reasoning accurately before responding
Avoid evidence

The sample may not represent the broader population identified in the claim.
The survey is invalid solely because it is voluntary.
The conclusion needs a longer title.
quiz.explanation: Sampling scope limits a general conclusion.

quiz.question: English IV · Week 13 (Argument Architecture: Claims, Evidence & Warrants): Which claim is proportionate to the evidence?

'The volunteers proved the change will work.'
'People not surveyed certainly felt the same.'
'Among the volunteers surveyed, most preferred the proposed schedule.'
quiz.explanation: The denominator and population match the actual evidence.

notes: The United States has no single federal national English curriculum. This course is designed for broad portability, rigorous senior readiness, and transparent local crosswalking—not automatic approval in every jurisdiction or program.

The course cross-aligns current Florida Grade 12 B.E.S.T. benchmarks, Common Core Grade 11–12 college- and career-readiness expectations, NAEP Grade 12 reading concepts, SAT/ACT domains, AP Language and AP Literature skill frameworks, and international language-and-literature reference points.
AP, IB, Cambridge, state diploma, district, umbrella-school, scholarship, accreditation, and transcript status require separate approval or verification where applicable.

Teachers should document instructional time, approved texts, accommodations, source permissions, student work, teacher-scored writing and speaking, assessment results, corrections, revision, and portfolio evidence.
